Issue: User Rights Assignments (~30 checks): Require manual review of Local Security Policy. These cannot be auto-evaluated because they depend on organizational role definitions (e.g., who should have "Debug programs" or "Act as part of the operating system" rights).
Recommendation: Recommend using the User and the Administrator groups. The user group would consist of the general user of the applications and is where majority of accounts get added. The administrator's group is for privileged users only. The administrators group consists of individuals tasked with maintaining and managing the system. Shared accounts are generally prohibited. If there is a situation where a shared account is needed, it needs to be documented with its purpose and who would require access.
Resolution: Implemented. Two local groups configured on the desktop: (1) Users group — general application operators who access Pytho via browser at http://localhost:8080. They are granted only "Allow log on locally" (V-253482). (2) Administrators group — restricted to personnel responsible for system maintenance, Docker/WSL management, and install.ps1 execution. All privileged rights (Debug programs V-253490, Back up files V-253483, Load device drivers V-253499, Take ownership V-253506, etc.) are assigned only to Administrators. High-severity rights — "Act as part of the operating system" (V-253481), "Create a token object" (V-253486), "Create permanent shared objects" (V-253488), "Lock pages in memory" (V-253500) — are not assigned to any group or account. No shared accounts exist. Each administrator has a named individual account for auditability. Reviewed and verified in Local Security Policy (secpol.msc).

Issue: Certificate store checks (~4 checks): DoD Root CA / Interoperability certificates must be visually verified in the certificate store. Not applicable in non-DoD environments.
Recommendation: While this is a DoD environment, the system will not be connected to the enterprise. DoD certificates are not required, and this can be documented.
Resolution: Documented. It is a standalone DoD workstation not connected to NIPR/SIPR or any enterprise network. No PKI-dependent services (smart card authentication, LDAP over TLS, domain trust chains) are in use. All application traffic is internal to the host — Docker containers communicate over the pytho-net bridge network and bind exclusively to 127.0.0.1. The following certificate checks are documented as not required for this deployment: V-253427 (DoD Root CA), V-253428 (External Root CA), V-253429 (DoD Interoperability Root CA cross-certificates), V-253430 (US DOD CCEB Interoperability Root CA). Documented for Authorizing Official (AO) awareness.

Issue: Organizational policy checks — ESS/Endpoint Security Software: These require human judgment and organizational policy decisions that cannot be automated.
Recommendation: ESS software in this scenario is not necessary since the system is standalone.
Resolution: Documented. Endpoint Security Software (ESS) such as HBSS/Trellix is not installed because this is a standalone system with no enterprise network connectivity, making centralized ESS management infrastructure (ePO server) unavailable. Compensating controls are in place: Windows Defender is active and running (V-253264 Pass), Windows Firewall is enabled on all profiles (V-253281 Pass), BitLocker encrypts all volumes (V-253259 Pass), AppLocker deny-all/permit-by-exception policy is active with 7 policies (V-253262 Pass), and all application ports bind to 127.0.0.1 only. Documented for AO awareness.

Issue: Organizational policy checks — Legal notice banners: These require human judgment and organizational policy decisions that cannot be automated.
Recommendation: Since this is a DoD system, the banner and legal notice need to be applied in the local group policy.
Resolution: Implemented. The DoD Warning Statement has been applied via Local Security Policy (secpol.msc) at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System. "Interactive logon: Message title for users attempting to log on" is set to "US Department of Defense Warning Statement". "Interactive logon: Message text for users attempting to log on" is set to the full DoD consent banner text. All users (both User and Administrator accounts) must acknowledge the banner by clicking OK before reaching the Windows login screen. Satisfies V-253445 (WN11-SO-000075) and V-253446 (WN11-SO-000080).

Issue: Organizational policy checks — Camera, Bluetooth, and WiFi policy: These require human judgment and organizational policy decisions that cannot be automated.
Recommendation: The policy surrounding camera, Bluetooth and WiFi is already in place. Currently, these items are not authorized for use within this facility. These items labeled as "Not A Finding" reference MCWL policies.
Resolution: Not A Finding. Per MCWL facility policy, camera, Bluetooth, and WiFi are not authorized for use within this facility. Camera is physically covered or disabled when not in use (V-253351). No Bluetooth hardware is detected on the desktop (V-253291 N/A, V-253293 N/A). WiFi is administratively prohibited. These controls are enforced by physical security and facility policy. No software configuration changes required.

Issue: Docker CIS 2.9 — User namespace remapping: Enabling user namespace remapping (userns-remap) breaks volume mount permissions for several of our containers (Elasticsearch, Stable Diffusion) that expect to write to mounted paths as specific UIDs. This is a known incompatibility with many third-party images.
Recommendation: This is something we need to ensure is in the documentation, so the authorizing official is aware.
Resolution: Documented — Risk Accepted. Enabling userns-remap causes UID mapping conflicts with: Elasticsearch (writes to /usr/share/elasticsearch/data as UID 1000), Stable Diffusion WebUI (writes models and outputs as root), and Kokoro TTS. These are third-party images with hardcoded UID expectations that cannot be changed without forking each image. Compensating controls: all containers run with no-new-privileges:true (configured in /etc/docker/daemon.json), privileged containers are not used (CIS 5.5 Pass), host namespaces are not shared (CIS 5.10/5.16/5.17 Pass), container root filesystems are read-only where possible (docker-api, nginx, es-secure all set read_only: true). Docker host is a single-purpose machine with one authorized admin user. Documented for AO awareness.

Issue: Docker CIS 2.12 — Docker client authorization: Authorization plugins add overhead and are designed for multi-tenant Docker hosts. This is a single-purpose machine with one user (pytho-mcwl), so the risk is accepted.
Recommendation: This is something we need to ensure is in the documentation, so the authorizing official is aware.
Resolution: Documented — Risk Accepted. Authorization plugins (e.g., Twistlock, Open Policy Agent) add latency to every Docker API call and are designed for environments where multiple untrusted users share a Docker daemon.The desktop is a single-purpose machine with one admin user and one standard user who accesses only via browser. The Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) is accessible only to root and the docker group inside WSL2 Ubuntu. No remote Docker API access is configured — Docker daemon does not listen on TCP (CIS 2.7 confirms). Documented for AO awareness.

Issue: Docker CIS 4.6 — Missing HEALTHCHECK: The three flagged images (elasticsearch, kokoro-fastapi-cpu, stable-diffusion-webui) are third-party images we do not control. Adding HEALTHCHECK would require forking/rebuilding each image.
Recommendation: If this is not required for the operation of the application, we can document this, so the authorizing official is aware.
Resolution: Documented — Risk Accepted. The three flagged images (docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:9.1.4, ghcr.io/remsky/kokoro-fastapi-cpu:v0.1.4, ghcr.io/ai-dock/stable-diffusion-webui:latest-cpu) are third-party images whose Dockerfiles we do not control. Adding HEALTHCHECK instructions would require forking and rebuilding each image, creating an ongoing maintenance burden for upstream updates. Compensating control: docker-compose.yml defines healthcheck directives at the compose level for all three services — Elasticsearch (curl http://localhost:9200/_cluster/health, 30s interval), Kokoro TTS (curl http://localhost:8880/, 30s interval), Stable Diffusion (curl http://localhost:17860/, 60s interval). This achieves equivalent runtime health monitoring, confirmed by CIS 5.27 (Pass). Documented for AO awareness.

Issue: Docker CIS 5.9 — Open ports: All flagged ports (7860, 8080, 8000, 9200, 9300) are required for application functionality. They are bound to the internal Docker network and accessed through the proxy.
Recommendation: This is something we need to ensure is in the documentation, so the authorizing official is aware.
Resolution: Documented — Risk Accepted. All ports are required for Pytho application functionality and are bound exclusively to 127.0.0.1 (loopback) — they are NOT accessible from the network. Port 8080/tcp: Nginx reverse proxy — serves the Pytho web UI and proxies all API requests to backend services. This is the single entry point for users. Port 8000/tcp: docker-api (Python/FastAPI) — backend service handling document processing, AI queries, text-to-speech, and image generation requests. Port 9200/tcp: Elasticsearch HTTP API — document search and indexing, authenticated via API key (not exposed to network). Port 9300/tcp: Elasticsearch transport — internal cluster communication protocol (single-node deployment). Port 7860/tcp: Stable Diffusion WebUI API — AI image generation endpoint, accessed only by docker-api container. Additional ports when optional services are deployed: 9845/tcp (geo-agent backend), 8765/tcp and 8766/tcp (coa-engine WebSocket and HTTP), 8880/tcp (Kokoro TTS). All container traffic stays on the pytho-net Docker bridge network. CIS 5.14 confirms all traffic is bound to a specific host interface (Pass). Documented for AO awareness.

Issue: Docker CIS 5.13 — Root FS read-write on stability_api: The Stable Diffusion WebUI container requires write access to its filesystem for model downloads and temporary file generation at runtime. Mounting read-only would break functionality.
Recommendation: This is something we need to ensure is in the documentation, so the authorizing official is aware.
Resolution: Documented — Risk Accepted. The Stable Diffusion WebUI container (stability_api) requires read-write root filesystem access for: (1) downloading model files (~5GB safetensors) to /opt/stable-diffusion-webui/models on first launch, (2) generating temporary files during image inference, (3) writing output images to /opt/stable-diffusion-webui/outputs. Setting read_only: true in docker-compose.yml causes the container to fail on startup. Compensating controls: all other containers run with read-only root filesystem (docker-api, nginx/proxy-app, es-secure all have read_only: true). The stability_api container is additionally constrained by: memory limit (64GB), CPU limit (8 cores), PID limit (300), no-new-privileges:true, port bound to 127.0.0.1:7860 only, and isolated on pytho-net Docker network. Documented for AO awareness.
